title: Central Registry Bottleneck (Merge-Conflict Architecture)
pattern: A single central module, enum, or `match` statement holds explicit references to every plug-in, command handler, or service in the system to dispatch requests.
why_bad: It creates a merge-conflict bottleneck. Adding a new feature or command forces developers to modify this central registry file. In a team environment, this leads to frequent Git merge conflicts on the registry file, slowing down development and coupling unrelated features to a single shared file.
detection: A central `match` statement or explicit registry map that lists every concrete handler type or enum variant in the application, requiring modification for every new feature introduction.
counterexample: A simple dispatcher where the set of commands is extremely small, static, and fundamentally guaranteed not to expand over the lifecycle of the program (e.g., standard CRUD actions).
fix: Decouple the dispatcher using dynamic registration. Let handlers register themselves automatically at startup using a generic Registry map (e.g., `HashMap<String, Box<dyn Command>>`), or utilize compile-time link-section registrations.
source: Mark Richards, Neal Ford, *Fundamentals of Software Architecture* (2020), Chapter 10 ("Microkernel Architecture"); Robert C. Martin, *Clean Architecture* (2017), Chapter 7 ("Symptom 2: Merges"), pp. 65-66.
